lesson.title: Roger Williams and the ‘Lively Experiment’ of Rhode Island
lesson.summary: Banished from Massachusetts Bay for preaching liberty of conscience and Native land rights, Roger Williams founded Providence in 1636 and built Rhode Island into colonial America's first haven for religious dissenters.
lesson.body:
Roger Williams arrived in the Massachusetts Bay Colony in February 1631, a young Puritan minister trained at Cambridge who quickly proved too radical even for a colony founded by religious dissenters. Invited to serve as teacher of the Boston church, he refused because the congregation had not formally separated from the Church of England. He moved instead to Salem and briefly to Plymouth, and everywhere he went his preaching grew more insistent on ideas that unsettled the colony's leaders.

Williams argued that civil government had no authority to punish people for their religious beliefs or to enforce worship, since the first four of the Ten Commandments concerned duties to God alone and lay beyond the reach of magistrates. He also insisted that the Massachusetts Bay charter was worthless because the king had granted land that belonged to Native peoples without ever purchasing it from them. Both positions struck directly at the foundations of the colony: its fusion of church and state, and its claim to the land itself. Because Massachusetts Bay Colony had been built on the premise that civil and religious order reinforced one another, Williams's ideas looked less like theological quibbling and more like a threat to the whole experiment.

The Massachusetts General Court banished Williams in October 1635. Warned that officials planned to ship him back to England, he fled south in the dead of winter, later recalling that he wandered for weeks without adequate food or shelter. He found refuge among Native communities, and in the spring of 1636 he purchased land from the Narragansett sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi at the head of Narragansett Bay. There he founded Providence, naming it for what he considered God's providential care during his exile, and declared it a haven where no one would be persecuted for matters of conscience.

Other exiles soon joined him. Followers of Anne Hutchinson, banished from Massachusetts in the Antinomian Controversy, founded Portsmouth in 1638 on Aquidneck Island, and Newport followed in 1639. Williams helped unite these scattered settlements first under a parliamentary patent in 1644 and then under a royal charter granted by Charles II in 1663, which guaranteed full liberty of conscience and prohibited any established church, an extraordinary provision for its time. In Providence in 1638 Williams also helped organize what is generally considered the first Baptist congregation in America, though he soon left organized religion altogether, calling himself a seeker.

Williams remained closely engaged with the Narragansett people throughout his life, learning their language well enough to publish A Key into the Language of America in 1643, a book that doubled as a phrasebook and an argument for Native humanity and dignity. Rhode Island's toleration made it a magnet for Quakers, Jews, and other groups unwelcome elsewhere in New England, and its founding stands as one of the earliest practical experiments in separating church authority from civil government in American history.
